advisor_letter:
Dear Patricia and James,

Carrying two generations at once — children heading toward university while an aging parent needs support — is one of the most demanding seasons a family budget faces, and planning your own retirement on top of it takes real resolve. The reassuring starting point is that you have **17** years before your target retirement and a shared, clear-eyed view of what matters.

You arrive here with roughly **$368K** built across your accounts as a couple, alongside well-defined family commitments. This report takes that full picture seriously — competing priorities and all — and reads it plainly rather than alarmingly.

The pages ahead cover your projected income, how long the savings would last, your family goals, and the scenarios where the plan holds versus where it tightens. I encourage particular attention to how the near-term family commitments sit alongside long-term saving.

Wishing you a clear and steady read. Consult a certified financial planner before acting on any observation in this report.
overall_assessment: In **5000** simulated futures, the couple's plan holds up in about **46%** of them — under strain, though with a long runway still ahead. Its main strength is a substantial combined asset base and **17** years to build on it, while its central vulnerability is the monthly gap between target spending and guaranteed income during the years family costs peak.
verdict: The spread of outcomes is wide — many paths exhaust savings while a favourable one preserves close to **$285K** — reflecting how much rides on the years when tuition and parent-care costs overlap with saving. That width is driven mainly by sequence-of-returns and the timing of those family outlays.
page_zero_verdict: What likely weighs on you both is whether supporting your children and your parent now will quietly cost you your own retirement later — and this report is built to look at that trade-off squarely.
profile_summary: Together Patricia and James hold **$368K** — a **$165K** RRSP, a **$42K** TFSA, and **$18K** non-registered, with **$110K** RRSP and **$28K** TFSA on the spousal side. The mix sits near **60.3%** equities and **39.7%** bonds, a growth-oriented posture that fits a **17**-year horizon while adding short-term variability.
trajectory_insight: In most scenarios the savings are drawn down over retirement, with durability near age **74** in the tighter paths, while public benefits continue beyond that point. The favourable cases hold up far longer, underlining how much the overlap of family spending and early-retirement returns shapes the result.
income_insight: Guaranteed income — combined CPP and OAS — is projected to cover about **61%** of the **$7,200** monthly spending target, leaving a gap of roughly **$4,975** a month for savings to fund. Combined CPP of **$4,169** and OAS of **$2,763** form a substantial base, but the wide gap reflects a lifestyle that the portfolio must work hard to support.
taxInsight: Lifetime tax is projected near **$964K** at an average effective rate of **14.5%**, with **0** years crossing the OAS clawback threshold. With most savings in registered accounts split across two spouses, coordinating withdrawals is where the meaningful efficiency lies.
estateInsight: The projections do not leave a net estate (**$0**) in the typical case, as savings are absorbed by retirement spending. A spousal rollover would defer any tax between Patricia and James, and the figure would rise in stronger market paths.
gis_insight: Modest Guaranteed Income Supplement eligibility appears in about **19** years of the projection, a secondary element rather than a central pillar at this income level. It could grow in later retirement as taxable income falls, but it is not what the plan depends on.
riskInsight: The plan is most sensitive to investment returns in the years just before and after retirement — a favourable one-point move adds roughly **$159K** — because the portfolio is doing heavy lifting against a wide income gap. Sequence-of-returns during that window is the factor most likely to decide whether the plan tightens or eases.
goals_insight: Both family goals look well supported despite the strain elsewhere: 'Children university tuition' of **$80K** at age **58** and 'Aging parent care contribution' of **$30K** at age **53** each carry roughly a **95%** probability of being met, with median amounts available well above the targets. This suggests the near-term commitments are fundable; the tension lies in protecting long-term retirement saving while they are met.
stress_interpretation: Across the stress tests the plan is sensitive to adverse environments — falling to about **16%** under stagflation and **23%** in a lost decade — with longevity and inflation pressing hardest. A sturdier path would take shape in stages: first, holding the family-cost years to plan; then, lifting the savings rate as those costs roll off; and finally, weighing a later retirement or deferred benefits. Consult a certified financial planner before acting on any observation in this report.
